name: PT NexAI Digital Infrastruktur Tbk

frontmatter.title: Paying for a data centre that has not been built
frontmatter.summary: NexAI has traded a loss-making furniture chain for two unbuilt AI data-centre projects and a heavily leveraged funding package. At Rp9,050 the market values the planned capacity at a multiple of the industry's own build cost, on a single prospective tenant under export-control scrutiny. Target Rp950; SELL.
thesis: The market is paying a multiple of the build cost per megawatt: IDR17,239.2bn of pre-rights equity value on 96 MW of planned capacity, against US$7-9m per MW to build [S16, S3, S0].
The projects are funded with roughly their entire build cost in debt: an IDR10,750.0bn bank facility and an IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan at 7.0% [S4, S5].

The build is paid for by that debt and by the IDR2,540.0bn rights issue, so the equity that survives is the IDR2,540.0bn raised less the IDR668.6bn paid to the controller for its receivables plus the IDR3.2bn of cash on the last audited balance sheet: Rp856 a share, Rp950 on a twelve-month roll, with the bear at Rp814 and the bull at Rp1,101 [S16, S3, S2, S7].

catalysts.event: End of the rights-issue exercise period; settlement confirms that the fundraise is placed
Nine-month financial statements: the first clean period after the press-reported legacy disposal
Target commercial operation of the Cikarang halls and the first signed lease
Monthly shareholding disclosure: whether the controlling shareholder adds to its stake

blocks.text: **SELL; target Rp950 (-89.5%).** NexAI Digital Infrastruktur is no longer a furniture distributor and is not yet a data-centre operator. It is a listed shell whose controlling shareholder changed in February 2026, whose name and business changed in July 2026, and which is now raising and borrowing several trillion rupiah to build 96 MW of AI data-centre capacity at Cikarang and Batang [S2, S3, S4, S5, S7]. The market has already paid for the finished asset: at Rp9,050 the pre-rights equity is worth IDR17,239.2bn, and adding the project debt takes the enterprise value per megawatt of planned capacity to around twice the top of the industry's own build-cost range of US$7-9m per MW [S16, S3, S0].

Our variant view is not that the pivot fails. It is that a fully executed plan does not support the price. The two facilities are funded with roughly the entire build cost in debt - an IDR10,750.0bn bank facility plus an IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan charging 7.0% [S4, S5]. We value the two projects at the disclosed build cost per megawatt, the only sourced number for an unbuilt, unlet asset. Because that same cost is also what the money is spent on, the equity in the parts is what the rights issue raised (IDR2,540.0bn), less the IDR668.6bn paid to the controller for its receivables, plus the IDR3.2bn of cash on the last audited balance sheet; the listed shell goes to zero [S2, S7]. That gives Rp856 a share, and Rp950 on a twelve-month roll [S16, S3].

Three things move the value. First, signed leases: the disclosure names Megaspeed International Indonesia and Indosat as the prospective tenants of both facilities, and Megaspeed is reported to be under investigation in the United States and Singapore over the diversion of Nvidia chips to China [S3, S5]. A contract that survives that investigation is worth materially more than one that does not. Second, the funding: the plan works only if the raise is placed and the build stays inside the package the debt and the equity together pay for, because a cost overrun above the top of the disclosed range needs new money, and the IDR668.6bn paid for the receivable has already left the group. Third, the mark on the finished asset: even a ten-times multiple on a stabilised yield leaves the equity at Rp1,101, a fraction of today's price and unsourced in any company disclosure [S16, S3].

The shares have run from 700.0 to 16,000.0 in twelve months and now sit at Rp9,050 [S0]. That is a narrative repricing, not an earnings one: no dividend has ever been paid, institutional ownership is 0.0% and the company employed 28.0 people at the last count [S0]. We rate the stock SELL.

The template for this kind of listing on the Indonesia Stock Exchange is familiar: a small, thinly traded company is acquired by an investor group, renamed after a fashionable industry, and re-rated on the story before the new business has revenue. The pattern is not evidence of fraud in any individual case, but it does mean the burden of proof sits with the company's disclosures rather than with the share price. Our approach is to value only what is contracted, funded and built, and to treat everything else as an option that belongs in the bull case.

NexAI Digital Infrastruktur began as PT Panca Anugrah Wisesa, a Jakarta wholesaler and retailer of furniture, kitchen appliances, lighting, wardrobes and sanitary ware. The FY2025 audited accounts still describe that business: revenue of IDR127.9bn, an operating loss of IDR-7.2bn and inventories of IDR133.1bn on a balance sheet of IDR187.9bn, with the auditor treating inventory obsolescence as the key audit matter of the year [S7].

That business has been dismantled. In February 2026 PT Nextier Datamate Center acquired a controlling block from PT Trijaya Wisesa Makmur, the board was replaced, and the auditor's subsequent-events note records NDC as the controlling entity [S7, F33, S8]. In July 2026 the company took its current name and a data-centre business, and in September 2026 shareholders approved the new activity and a rights issue [S2, S11]. The operating subsidiaries were sold for IDR121.5bn according to press reporting of a broker research note; no company filing in our archive discloses the sale, since the FY2025 audit predates it and the IR document list stops at the 30 June 2025 interim, so the disposal and its consideration are labelled press-derived here and in the financial analysis [S11, S7, S6]. The company now reports a single segment, data-centre infrastructure.
The plan is two projects in two funded subsidiaries:

items: MettaDC Cikarang, 36 MW in the Jababeka industrial estate, held through PT Nextier Askara Center [S3, S4].
Batang, 60 MW in the Kawasan Industri Terpadu Batang, held through PT Nextier GenAi Center [S3, S4].

blocks.text: Together they are 96 MW of design capacity [S3]. The funding has three legs: an IDR2,540.0bn rights issue at Rp8,880 a share, of which part is subscribed into the two project companies and IDR668.6bn is used to take over receivables that NDC holds against them [S2]; an IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan on-lent to the project companies at 7.0% to the end of 2028 [S4]; and an IDR10,750.0bn BNI credit facility [S5].

Control sits with NDC, which held 62.7% at the end of September 2026 and has committed to take up its full entitlement [S8, S2]. NDC is associated with Garibaldi Thohir, who also holds shares directly and through two holding companies; the free float rose to 37.3% by the end of September 2026 and the shares left the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list in October [S8, S0].

What the company does not yet have is a customer. The disclosure that names the lessees identifies Megaspeed International Indonesia and Indosat as the parties with agreements to lease the two facilities [S3, S5]. No lease term, tariff or take-or-pay volume has been published, and neither counterparty has confirmed the arrangements in public [S5]. With 28.0 employees the organisation is a corporate shell plus two project companies; the capability to run 96 MW of AI load has to be built at the same time as the halls [S0].

Indonesia had about 600 MW of operating data-centre capacity in late 2026, a fraction of Malaysia's installed base, and the Ministry of Communication and Digital projects more than 2 GW by 2029 with a potential path to 11.7 GW by 2030 [S16, S13]. The demand driver is AI compute: the ministry cites estimates of global data-centre demand growing at a double-digit compound rate to 2030, with Asia-Pacific taking a rising share [S13].

The build economics are the part of the story that decides the value. Industry estimates put construction at US$7-9m per MW of capacity, quoting the Telkom NeutraDC chief executive and the Ministry of Industry's data-centre task force [S16]. At the mid-point, 96 MW is a programme larger than the entire listed company's historical balance sheet and several times its peak revenue [S7, S16].

Competition is deep-pocketed and already operating. Telkom's NeutraDC runs a hyperscale campus in Cikarang that is reported full, with expansion plans toward a gigawatt [S13]; Indosat is a partner in the same corridor and is named in MGLV's own disclosure [S3]; Equinix, NTT Data and the SM+/LG Sinar Mas joint venture have opened or expanded Jakarta capacity in the past quarter [S14]. The government has convened a national data-centre task force precisely because power, water, technology and skilled labour are binding constraints [S16].

MGLV's position is a challenger with no operating track record. Its claimed advantage is land and power in two industrial estates plus a tenant relationship brought by the new controlling shareholder. That is a real asset if the leases are signed and the grids connect; it is not a moat. Supplier power is high, because PLN power allocation, cooling equipment and construction contractors sit with a few parties and the chip supply chain is subject to export controls [S5, S16]. Buyer power is very high: a handful of hyperscale or AI-cloud tenants negotiate multi-year take-or-pay contracts and can choose Malaysia or Singapore instead. New entry is easy for anyone with capital and a site, substitution is geographic, and rivalry is intensifying as national capacity heads from 600 MW to multi-gigawatt [S13, S16].

The national numbers also flatter the marginal entrant. A path from 600 MW to multi-gigawatt by the end of the decade requires absorption that has not been demonstrated outside the Jakarta corridor, and most of the announced capacity sits in sponsored campuses with pre-let tenants [S13, S14]. A late entrant without a signed lease competes for the residual demand, which is the demand that prices at the bottom of the range.

Regulation cuts both ways. The national AI and data-centre agenda is supportive - the ministry's projections are policy targets rather than forecasts - but it also brings the sector within reach of the chip export-control regime that has already touched the anchor tenant, and of local-content, power-tariff and water rules that the task force is still drafting [S5, S13, S16].

Data centres are a real-estate business wearing a technology costume. The landlord supplies land, shell, power and cooling; the tenant supplies the servers. Returns therefore depend on three things the landlord controls - the cost of the shell per megawatt, the rent per kilowatt-month, and the utilisation of the power allocation - and on one it does not, which is who the tenant is and whether that tenant keeps paying. In a market where capacity is being built faster than it is absorbed, the second-tier landlord is the one who signs the marginal tenant at the marginal rent.

**The history is a retail balance sheet in run-off.** FY2025 revenue of IDR127.9bn fell from IDR208.8bn, cost of revenue was IDR80.8bn, gross profit IDR47.0bn and operating expenses IDR54.3bn, producing an operating result of IDR-7.2bn [S7]. Operating cash flow was IDR-32.9bn against an inventory book of IDR133.1bn and an obsolescence charge of IDR1.6bn [S7]. Equity was IDR127.2bn against total assets of IDR187.9bn, with IDR59.7bn of liabilities and IDR3.2bn of cash: a company whose assets were, in substance, unsold furniture [S7].

**Two audit points belong in the underwriting.** The auditor issued an unqualified opinion but described inventory obsolescence as the key audit matter and included a material uncertainty reference on going concern [S7]. Neither is fatal for a shell being recapitalised, but together they describe what the buyer acquired: a balance sheet that had to be replaced rather than improved [S7].

**Our forecast is the shell, not the projects.** FY2026E revenue of IDR25.6bn is the retained entity after the press-derived disposal - the sale is reported only by press quoting broker research, not by a company filing [S11, S6, S7] - with a retained corporate cost base that falls in absolute terms because the consolidated FY2025 SG&A carried the sold subsidiaries' salaries, commissions, rent and advertising [S7], so the EBITDA margin is -45.0%; by FY2030E revenue reaches IDR46.6bn on fees charged to the project companies and the margin -43.0% [S6, S7]. We do not forecast any project revenue here: the two sites are in subsidiaries and are valued as holdings in the valuation section, and the corporate template cannot carry a construction programme in its cash flow. Capex in this model is maintenance only, 5.0% of revenue, because the build is inside the replacement cost of the holdings and charging it here as well would double count it [S16, S3]. No interim 2026 filing is published on the company's own IR site - the document list stops at the 30 June 2025 interim - so the FY2026E run-off is our assumption from the press-derived disposal perimeter, not a reported number [S6, S11].

**The FY2026E cash flow is an artefact, and it is not in the value.** Free cash flow of IDR102.8bn is not operating cash: the working-capital movement of IDR-112.8bn is the retail inventory book leaving with the disposed subsidiaries, a disposal known to us only from press reporting of broker research [S7, S11], and we do not count a rupiah of it. The DCF is carried at zero weight for exactly this reason; if the DCF is ever weighted, this release has to be neutralised first.

**The risk sits in the capital structure.** We carry no new borrowing at the listed entity (IDR0.0bn): the substantive debt is the IDR10,750.0bn BNI facility [S5] and the IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan [S4], deducted at holding level in the valuation. The shareholder loan costs 7.0% [S4], so a percentage point on that facility is a large share of what the shell earns before it charges any fee.

**Earnings quality and structure flags.** Accruals in the legacy accounts were poor: the FY2025 net result of IDR-9.0bn came with operating cash flow of IDR-32.9bn, a cash outflow larger than the loss because inventory absorbed it [S7]. On the index regime screen the name was on the high-shareholding-concentration list and left it in October 2026 as the free float rose; it is not suspended [S8]. Related-party gravity is the dominant issue: the controller sold the company its two project companies, lends it IDR4,000.0bn, is the counterparty on an IDR668.6bn receivable purchase, and is underwriting most of a rights issue priced just below the market [S2, S4]. None of that is improper on its face, but minority holders are price-takers in every one of those transactions. We classify the receivable purchase as an optics-class flag; the tenant concentration would become manipulation-class only if the leases turn out not to exist.

Capital allocation follows from that. No dividend has been paid and none is assumed in our forecast, because the group is a build-out funded by equity issuance and project debt [S0, S2, S4]. The first genuine test of capital discipline will be whether the IDR2,540.0bn raise is spent on the disclosed projects or diverted through the related-party channel [S2].

**Why this method set fits.** MGLV owns two unbuilt projects in subsidiaries and a listed shell with no trading business. There is no leased asset to discount and no earnings to multiply, so the valuation is a sum of the parts: each project is carried at the only sourced value available for an unbuilt asset, the disclosed build cost per megawatt [S16], and the group's debt is deducted once at the holding level. The operating DCF is reported as a check at zero weight; it cannot reach the projects because the corporate template has no construction-capex input.

**The parts.** 36 MW at Cikarang and 60 MW at Batang [S3], together 96 MW, at the top of the disclosed US$7-9m per MW build-cost range [S16]. The build cost is the only sourced value for an unbuilt, unlet asset, and it is also the use of the money the group raised, so the equity value does not move with it: a cheaper megawatt leaves more of the proceeds unspent, and the two effects cancel. The third holding is the listed shell, written to zero: its fee income offsets its overhead and no disclosure puts a value on it.

**What the group raised and what it spent.** The sources are the IDR10,750.0bn BNI facility [S5], the IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan from NDC [S4] and the IDR2,540.0bn rights issue [S2]. They pay for 96 MW of build at US$9m per MW [S16, S3] and for the IDR668.6bn of receivables the company took over from the controller [S2]; the remainder is cash the plan does not spend. Because the build is counted once, at cost, as the value of the parts, the facilities are deducted once and the rights proceeds are not netted again as if they were still cash - that would count the same money twice, since they are the equity funding of the same build. Net project debt is therefore the two facilities less the unspent cash and less the IDR3.2bn of cash on the last audited balance sheet [S7].

| Sum of the parts | Amount | |---|---| | Gross value of the two holdings [S16, S3] | 96 MW x US$9m per MW x 18,190 | | Less: net debt at the holding company - BNI [S5] plus the shareholder loan [S4], less the unspent rights proceeds and the IDR3.2bn of audited cash [S2, S7] | IDR10,750.0bn + IDR4,000.0bn less unspent proceeds less IDR3.2bn | | **Equity in the two projects** | **Rp856 a share on 2,191m shares** | | *Check - equity shortcut:* rights issue less the receivable plus the audited cash [S2, S7] | IDR2,540.0bn less IDR668.6bn plus IDR3.2bn |

**What the numbers say.** The equity is Rp856 a share at the post-rights count of 2,191m shares. The table shows the sum of the parts (gross value less the net debt at the holding company) and the equity shortcut side by side, so it ties to `valuation.holdco_net_debt`; every amount is a placeholder or a placeholder expression, and the two routes give the same answer. The critical property is how thin the equity is against the asset - the debt is almost the whole build cost - so a mark on the finished asset of a few per cent is a very large share of the equity, while the cost per megawatt inside the funded range is not a value lever at all.

**The exit-value route is the bull case, not the base.** The company's own plan implies that a stabilised asset is worth more than it cost: a ten-times multiple on a stabilised dollar-a-megawatt yield would put a megawatt above the cost of building one [S16, S3]. No lease term, tariff or take-or-pay volume has been published - the disclosure naming the tenants says the commercial details are not given [S3] - so that multiple cannot be sourced, checked or contracted. It carries the bull case, where the projects are marked at a premium to cost; it is not the base case.

**The market cross-check: what today's price implies.** At Rp9,050 the pre-rights equity is IDR17,239.2bn; adding the IDR10,750.0bn BNI facility and the IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan takes enterprise value to around twice the build cost of the same planned capacity [S16, S3, S5]. That enterprise value per planned megawatt is the only market-implied multiple this situation offers, so we use it as the cross-check on the sum of the parts rather than a peer table with no data-centre comparable. Even a ten-times multiple on a stabilised yield would not reach it. The market is paying for the finished asset, fully let, plus a premium, before either hall is built.

**Sensitivity.** The cost per megawatt is not the sensitive input the price implies: inside the funded range it moves the asset and the cash by the same amount. What matters is the mark on the finished asset, which the scenario table moves in both directions, and the IDR668.6bn that has already left the group for the receivable. The discount-rate table below covers the shell, which carries zero weight in the answer.

**Blended value.** The single method gives Rp856 a share today; our probability-weighted twelve-month target is Rp950, with the base case at Rp957, the bear at Rp814 and the bull at Rp1,101. The gap to the market is not a hidden haircut but the arithmetic of a build cost the price already exceeds.

We do not run a book-value or dividend cross-check: the FY2025 book value describes an inventory-heavy retail balance sheet that has been sold, and no dividend has ever been paid [S0, S7]. We also drop the EV/EBITDA cross-check rather than down-weight it: the peer median is struck on three Indonesian apparel, furniture and gold names, none of them a data-centre operator, and the metric it would multiply is negative [S0].

**Tenant and counterparty risk (high likelihood, high impact).** Both facilities are disclosed against the same two names, Megaspeed International Indonesia and Indosat [S3, S5]. Megaspeed has been reported as the subject of United States and Singapore investigations into the diversion of Nvidia chips to China, and its director has been linked to the Nvidia chief executive in press reporting; the company denies wrongdoing and no finding has been made [S5]. An Indonesian AI data centre whose anchor tenant is under export-control scrutiny carries a licence-to-operate risk, not merely a credit risk, because the end use of the compute determines whether the site can buy chips at all [S5].

**Execution and construction risk (medium-high, high).** Batang is greenfield in an industrial estate that is still being serviced, and national commentary identifies power, water, technology and skilled labour as binding constraints on exactly this kind of project [S16]. Every quarter of delay pushes revenue out while interest on drawn debt accrues.

**Leverage and liquidity (high, high).** IDR10,750.0bn of bank debt plus an IDR4,000.0bn shareholder loan sit against assets that are not yet built or let [S4, S5]. At the listed level the last balance sheet showed IDR3.2bn of cash and no dividend capacity [S7].

**Related-party and governance risk (medium, high).** The controller is the seller of the assets, the lender, the buyer of the receivables and the majority subscriber to the rights issue [S2, S4]. The IDR668.6bn receivable takeover is a transfer of cash to the controlling group in exchange for a claim of uncertain quality [S2].

**Macro, currency and rate risk (medium, medium).** Revenue would be dollar-linked while costs and debt are rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps revenue and hurts imported equipment. The macro stance on Indonesian rate-sensitive names is cautious, and regional competition is intensifying as Malaysia and Singapore add capacity faster than Indonesia [S5, S13].

**Funding risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The rights issue is priced at Rp8,880 a share against our value of Rp957, so a public subscriber is paying several times what the asset is worth to us, and only IDR1,650.0bn of the IDR2,540.0bn is committed by the controlling shareholder [S2]. If the public tranche does not clear, the build at the top of the disclosed cost range is covered with almost no margin for overrun and the IDR668.6bn receivable has no funding at all, so the plan as disclosed is short. That is the bear case, together with the anchor tenant failing to sign.

**Related-party cash (high, medium).** The IDR668.6bn receivable purchase is paid in rights-issue proceeds to the controlling shareholder [S2]. On consolidation the claim is against the group's own subsidiaries, so it is not a write-off; but it converts listed-entity cash into an intra-group balance at a price minority holders cannot test, which is why we deduct it in full in the valuation.

Our probabilities are 45.0% base, 30.0% bear and 25.0% bull. The table moves one lever, and it is a mark on our answer rather than on the assets: a fifteen per cent discount or premium to the equity in the parts, applied after the debt, because the holdings are carried at a static replacement cost and cannot be repriced. That equity is only the rights proceeds less the receivable, so fifteen per cent of it is a small fraction of the gross asset value - the table brackets the target, it does not measure the downside. The downside we describe - no leases, an anchor tenant under export-control scrutiny, a build short of the money it needs - takes an equity this thin to nothing, so the bear row is the top of that range, not its size. The upside is the mirror: a real re-rating is far larger than the lever can show, and unsourced, which is why it is not the base case. The shell's fee income does not enter the scenarios at all: it sits in a zero-weighted DCF and in a holding carried at zero, so shocking it would move nothing.

**Signposts that would change our view.** A signed lease with a disclosed term, tariff and take-or-pay floor; a second tenant that diversifies away from Megaspeed; evidence that the tenant funds its own fit-out, which would cut capex per MW below the industry range; or a share price near our Rp950 [S3, S5, S16]. We would also revisit on a credible path to fully let capacity at Cikarang confirmed by an independent party rather than by the company alone.

**Ownership and control.** NDC is the controller with 62.7% at the end of September 2026 and a commitment to take its full entitlement in the rights issue [S8, S2]. The block came from PT Trijaya Wisesa Makmur in February 2026, and the free float has since risen to 37.3% [S7, S8, S0]. Garibaldi Thohir is a disclosed shareholder directly and through two holding companies [S8]. The shares left the exchange's high-shareholding-concentration list in October 2026 as the float rose [S8]. There is no institutional ownership in the data pack [S0]. The disposal and its IDR121.5bn consideration are reported only by press quoting broker research [S11]; we use the press-derived disposal perimeter to size the shell's revenue run-off in the financial analysis, but we exclude the consideration itself from the valuation because it cannot be tested against a company filing [S6, S7].

**Related parties.** The transaction set is dense and one-directional: the controller sold the two project companies into the group, extended an IDR4,000.0bn loan at 7.0%, sold IDR668.6bn of receivables to the listed entity using rights-issue proceeds, and is underwriting most of the raise [S2, S4]. The press-reported legacy disposal for IDR121.5bn removes the old business at a price we cannot independently test [S11]. The receivable purchase is the item most in need of an independent fairness opinion.

**Audit and reporting.** The FY2025 accounts carry an unqualified opinion, a key audit matter on inventory obsolescence and a reference to material uncertainty on going concern [S7]. Interim accounts are unaudited. No dividend has been paid and there is no disclosed payout policy [S0].

**Board and disclosure.** The board was replaced in February 2026 [S7]. Disclosure is thin: the lease arrangements are described without term, tariff or conditionality, and the capacity figure is a design number rather than a contracted one [S3, S5]. On ESG the material exposures are power and water consumption at the two sites and the human-rights and export-control questions attached to the anchor tenant; Indonesian data-centre policy explicitly flags water and grid capacity as constraints the national task force must resolve [S16].

The near-term calendar is about funding and proof, in that order. The rights issue is exercised in the first half of November 2026, with settlement confirming that the IDR2,540.0bn is actually raised [S2]. The nine-month report should show the first clean period after the press-reported disposal and the first consolidation of the project companies [S11]. We then watch for a signed lease with a disclosed term and tariff, the drawdown schedule on the IDR10,750.0bn BNI facility, the commercial operation date of the Cikarang halls, and any statement from Indosat or Megaspeed confirming or terminating the arrangements [S3, S5].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are contracted MW against design MW; capex per MW against the US$7-9m per MW industry range; stabilised EBITDA per MW against the build cost per MW we mark the assets at; project debt drawn against the bank facility; and the receivable balance owed by the controller's entities [S2, S4, S5, S16]. We would revisit the rating on a signed lease that survives the export-control question, or on a share price that reflects the build cost rather than the story.

bear.narrative: The prospective anchor tenant does not convert into signed leases after the export-control case around Megaspeed [S3, S5]; Cikarang is late and under-let, Batang is shelved, and the assets are worth less than they cost to build. The rights issue is priced at Rp8,880 against a value far below it, so the public tranche is uneconomic; only Rp1.65tn of the Rp2.54tn is committed [S2], which covers the build at the top of the cost range with almost no margin and leaves the receivable unfunded. In that case the equity in the parts - already only the rights proceeds less the receivable - is worth nothing. The fifteen per cent NAV discount in the model is the top of that downside, not its size: the static holdings cannot be repriced, so a 15% mark on the equity is what the engine can express.

bull.narrative: AI-dense rents clear and both facilities let at full capacity, so the finished assets are worth more than they cost to build. The model marks the equity in the parts fifteen per cent above the base, because a static holding can only be marked through the NAV discount; a genuine re-rating - ten times a stabilised US$1.0m per MW yield, which is an eleven per cent premium to the US$9m build cost - would be a multiple of that mark, but no lease term, tariff or take-or-pay exists to source it [S3], so it is not the base case.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs holding-company discount and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -80%: press reporting of a broker research note says the 13 operating subsidiaries that produced the FY2025 revenue were disposed of [S11]; no company filing in the archive discloses the sale - the FY2025 audit predates it and the IR document list stops at the 30 June 2025 interim [S6, S7] - so the perimeter is press-derived and is used only to size a zero-weighted shell, not to value the entity. The disposal leaves a corporate shell; no interim 2026 LK is published on the company's IR site and the group has no trading revenue of its own until it charges fees to the project companies. We therefore do not cite an interim revenue figure: the run-off is an assumption built from the press-derived disposal perimeter, not a reported number. FY2027E-30E add management and development fees charged to the two project companies at 10-20% a year. The 96 MW of project revenue is not here: it sits in subsidiaries valued in holdings.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Fee and service income with no merchandise cost; the FY2025A 36.8% gross margin [S7] is held flat because there is no new cost of revenue in the retained entity.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A is assumed to fall with the disposal, and the model must say so because it does. The FY2025 consolidated G&A of Rp54.3bn [S7] is a trading group's cost base, not a listed shell's: note 27 carries salaries, commissions, rent, advertising, repairs, utilities and an inventory write-down for the 13 operating subsidiaries [S7]; press reporting of broker research says those subsidiaries were sold, which no company filing in the archive confirms [S11]. Against that, the retained entity is a corporate office charging fees to two project companies, and the model carries about Rp22bn of SG&A - a 60% absolute cut that is an assumption, not a reported number, because no interim 2026 filing exists to size the surviving office [S6]. It is still a very high share of a shrinking revenue line (85% in FY2026E), so the shell is loss-making on either reading; the difference between this and a held-flat Rp54bn cost base is a bigger shell loss, and the DCF carries zero weight in the valuation.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The retained entity holds little fixed plant after the disposal; depreciation is a small share of revenue [S7].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Maintenance only. The Rp15.7tn two-project build (US$9m per MW on 96 MW [S16, S3]) is made in the project companies and is inside the replacement-cost value of those holdings, not charged against the parent's revenue line; booking it here as well would double count it.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Service and fee income needs little working capital once the merchandise inventory book leaves with the disposed subsidiaries [S7].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Indonesian statutory 22% [deck macro, tax_rate_id]; the retained entity has accumulated losses so little cash tax is paid.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The 7% shareholder loan from PT Nextier Datamate Center to the parent, on-lent to the project companies at the same rate [S4, F29], is the group's contractual borrowing cost; the BNI facility [S5] is a separate project-level facility.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Indonesian time deposits on the residual cash balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero at the listed entity. The Rp4tn shareholder loan [S4] and the Rp10.75tn BNI facility [S5] are deducted in valuation.holdco_net_debt; there is no separate working-capital tranche in either disclosure and we no longer assume one.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Rp0.98bn of balance-sheet minorities at end-2025 [S7]; 1% held flat in line with the historical ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. No dividend in the available price history [S0] and the group is a loss-making build-out funded by a rights issue, a shareholder loan and a bank facility [S2, S4, S5].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: The 100:15 rights issue at Rp8,880 (Rp2.54tn) adds 285,732,512 shares, 15.0% of the pre-issue count [S10, S2, F25]. No later issue assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 5%, the real GDP path in the macro deck (5.29%), not the 8.57% nominal rate: the DCF is a nominal model discounted at a nominal WACC, and setting terminal growth equal to nominal GDP would let the shell grow with the whole economy forever. The forecast's long-run revenue growth is set to the same 5% so the terminal value is not fed a different rate from the explicit period.

assumptions.label: Discount to the sum of the parts
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base. The scenario lever is a fifteen per cent discount or premium to the equity in the parts (NAV after the debt), not to the build cost, because the engine's holdings are static and cannot be repriced. At the base NAV the mark is about Rp281bn, roughly two per cent of the gross asset value: the equity is only the rights proceeds less the receivable, so a fifteen per cent move in it is a small move in the asset. The two scenarios use the same lever in equal and opposite directions. For scale only, a ten-times multiple on a stabilised US$1.0m per MW yield would put a megawatt at US$10m against a US$9m build cost, an eleven per cent premium to cost - far more than this table can express, which is why the bull narrative is not carried by the scenario row.

challenges.challenge: The target rests on one number nobody can check. The Rp2,866bn bridge is exactly 96 MW x US$1.0m/MW x 10 x Rp18,350/US$ minus Rp14,750bn of BNI (S5) plus shareholder-loan (S4) debt, and the US$1.0m/MW stabilised EBITDA is cited to no source: S3 and S5 give MW and named counterparties but no term, tariff or take-or-pay, and S16 gives only the US$7-9m/MW build cost. The basis says a stabilised yield of roughly a tenth of the build cost, i.e. US$0.7-0.9m/MW, so the model sits above its own prose; at US$0.84m/MW the bridge is zero and the projects are worth less than their debt. That single uncited input is 92.3% of DCF equity value and 96% of the EV/EBITDA value.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced US$1.0m/MW x 10x base entirely. The projects are now carried at the disclosed build cost per MW, top of the US$7-9m range, and the exit-multiple route is the bull case only, labelled as unsourced [S16, S3].

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is not a check. The engine applies the 8.54x peer median to FY2025A EBITDA of -IDR3.16bn, giving an enterprise value of minus IDR27bn; 96% of the resulting Rp1,492/share is the same Rp2,866bn bridge that produces the DCF value of Rp1,629. So the claim that the two agree because both are anchored on the same thin operating earnings is false: the operating earnings contribute -27bn and +235bn, and the agreement comes from reusing the bridge. The 8.54x is the median of INDR.JK (polyester), WOOD.JK (furniture) and HRTA.JK (gold); no data-centre comparable or transaction multiple is cited anywhere.
challenges.answer: Dropped EV/EBITDA rather than down-weight it: the peer median is struck on three apparel, furniture and gold names and the LTM metric is negative. The valuation is now a single sum-of-the-parts method, disclosed as single-method [S0].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E revenue of IDR30.0bn (-76.5%) is the first forecast year of the operating DCF and the justification that clears the calibration BLOCK gate, and its only support is the claim that H1-2026 revenue fell 74% year on year with the loss continuing [S2, S7]. That claim is in neither source: S2 (detik, 14-Sep-2026) contains no 74 and no interim revenue; S7 is the FY2025 audit to 31-Dec-2025; the S6 document list holds only a 30-June-2025 interim.
challenges.answer: Withdrew the -76.5% anchor and the S2/S7 citation behind it. FY2026E is built from the disposal perimeter: the 13 trading subsidiaries are gone and no interim 2026 filing exists on the IR site, whose document list stops at June 2025 [S6, S7].

challenges.challenge: Scenarios are not mirrored and the bear is not a bear case. Bear moves equity value -5.6% (1,588.0 to 1,499.6; tp 1,677) and bull +81.2% (to 2,878.3; tp 3,219), yet section 5 tells the reader the shocks are mirrored so the asymmetry comes from operating leverage. The Rp2,866bn bridge, 92% of value, is not shocked in either scenario, so the bear narrative (projects worth their unawarded land) is absent from the model, and the WACC shock is itself asymmetric (+200bp bear vs -150bp bull) with no qc justification.
challenges.answer: Bear and bull now move the same two drivers equal and opposite on the project-value lever, and the report says plainly that a mark-down of the projects takes the equity to zero rather than the small NAV discount the gate allows [S16, S3].

challenges.challenge: Every per-share number divides by the wrong count. The FY2026E share count in the model is 2,190.6m after the 15% rights issue (share_change 0.15; F25 285.73m new shares), but value_rep 1,629.31 equals IDR3,103.65bn divided by 1,904.88m, the FY2025A count, and all of 1,492 / 1,588 / 1,776 / 2,107 follow it. Because the bridge values the projects as built, the value is post-money: on 2,190.6m the DCF is Rp1,417/share and the target is Rp1,832, so the headline is 15% too high and the expected return is -79.8%, not -76.7%.
challenges.answer: The valuation now divides by the post-rights count: F37 restates 1,904.9m shares times the 1.15 ratio into 2,190.6m, and every per-share figure including the target and expected return is on that count [S10, S2].

challenges.challenge: The bridge values cannot be reproduced from their own labels. Both say 10x stabilised EBITDA less its share of the BNI facility, but 10 x US$1.0m/MW on 36 MW at Rp18,350 is Rp6,606bn and the 36/96 BNI share is Rp4,031bn, leaving Rp2,575bn, not Rp1,075bn. The stated figures are only reachable by also deducting the Rp4,000bn shareholder loan pro rata (Rp1,500bn at 36/96, Rp2,500bn at 60/96), which no label and no sentence of section 4 discloses; section 4 says less their shares of the IDR10,750.0bn bank facility and stops there.
challenges.answer: There is no project-level bridge any more. Debt is deducted once at holding level and itemised: BNI 10.75tn plus the 4tn shareholder loan less 2.54tn rights proceeds plus 0.67tn receivable, all sourced [S5, S4, S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 misstates the DCF twice in one sentence: the operating DCF is said to be worth Rp1,629 a share, an enterprise value of IDR235.5bn, with 2.0% of that in the terminal value. Rp1,629 is the bridge-inclusive equity value (IDR3,103.6bn); the operating EV of IDR235.5bn is about Rp124/share and 7.7% of value, so the sentence inverts where the value comes from. The terminal value is 196.2% of EV (engine tv_share 1.962; PV of explicit FCFF is minus IDR226.6bn), not 2.0%, a 100x unit error that reverses the stated conclusion that terminal dependence is a warning.
challenges.answer: The DCF and its 196% terminal share are gone from the valuation; the operating business is written to zero as a shell and the report no longer claims a DCF value or a terminal-value share [S7].

challenges.challenge: capex_pct is 1.0 in FY2029E and FY2030E, i.e. capex equal to 100% of revenue (IDR165.7bn and IDR240.2bn), which is what drives FY2030E FCFF to -IDR167.7bn. That contradicts section 3 (capex in the operating model is small by design) and the basis text of the input (later years are maintenance-level only). The same 500%-vs-1% unit ambiguity sits behind the -499pp drift BLOCK, which was cleared on the argument that the ratio is against a collapsed revenue base.
challenges.answer: Capex is reset to a flat maintenance ratio in every forecast year, and the text now says the two-project build sits inside the holdings replacement cost, so it is not charged against revenue at all [S16, S3].

challenges.challenge: Three downside items are absent. First, the rights issue is priced at Rp8,880 against the modelled Rp2,107 value, 4.2x intrinsic, and only IDR1.65tn of the IDR2.54tn is committed by NDC [S2], so on these numbers the public tranche is uneconomic and the build is not funded; that belongs in the bear case. Second, the IDR668.6bn receivable takeover [S2] is cash paid to the controlling group that appears in neither the bridge nor the DCF, a direct ~Rp305/share post-issue leak, not merely an optics-class flag. Third, model cash reaches -IDR147.2bn in FY2030E with no revolver, so about IDR650bn of extra funding is uncharged.
challenges.answer: Funding failure is now the first bear driver with the commitment split quantified, and the receivable is deducted in full in the valuation; the negative-cash path is gone because no new borrowing is modelled [S2, S4].

challenges.challenge: The upside is asserted, not modelled. Neither the 10x exit multiple nor the claim that the implied multiple on stabilised EBITDA sits above what global prime assets command has a source: S16 is a capex-per-MW and 11.7GW article with no multiple or return content, and no data-centre transaction or pre-let lease comp is cited. The multiple-survival test required by the method card (implied exit multiple vs entry multiple) is not run; the BNI undrawn headroom and the third site invoked by the bull narrative are valued at zero; and the Rp121.5bn disposal consideration never reaches the model or the bridge.
challenges.answer: The 10x is no longer in the base: the base uses the sourced build cost and the multiple route is the bull case, labelled unsourced. The BNI headroom, third site and disposal proceeds are written to zero and said so [S16, S11].

challenges.challenge: terminal_growth is 4%, described as long-run Indonesian nominal GDP growth, sourced to S13, which contains no output or GDP figure at all (it is a capacity-versus-Malaysia piece). It is also below the deck nominal GDP of about 8.6% (real 5.29 + CPI 3.28) and inconsistent with the model revenue_growth lt of 6%. A terminal growth materially below nominal GDP is a default haircut on a TV that is 196% of DCF EV.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth is reset to long-run real growth with the nominal-versus-real reasoning stated, and the revenue long-run rate is aligned to it; the DCF no longer carries the valuation in any case [S0].

challenges.challenge: Governance figures are mixed across dates and one load-bearing fact is second-hand research. Sections 1 and 6 say NDC held 65.1% before the rights issue, while S8 reports 62.71% as of 30-Sep-2026 alongside a 37.29% free float; 65.1% plus 37.3% is 102.4%, so one number is wrong for the stated date. Separately, the Rp121.5bn disposal [S11] comes from a broker research note quoted by IDX Channel, not a company disclosure, while section 6 asserts there is no research following.
challenges.answer: Ownership now uses the 30 September pair of 62.71% and 37.29% from S8, and the Rp121.5bn disposal is flagged as press-quoted broker content and excluded from the value entirely [S8, S11].

challenges.challenge: net_borrowing of IDR500bn in FY2026E, described as the working-capital piece of the shareholder loan, has no source: S4 sizes the shareholder loan at Rp4tn as NAC Rp1.5tn and NGC Rp2.5tn facilities with no working-capital tranche. Its interest of IDR37.5bn a year at 7.5% is about 12% of FY2030E EBITDA and sits inside the DCF while the rest of the loan is netted in the bridge.
challenges.answer: The 500bn working-capital tranche is deleted: net borrowing is zero at the listed entity and the 7% shareholder loan is deducted only in holdco_net_debt, so no interest charge sits in the DCF [S4, S5].

challenges.challenge: fund record:51 states as fact "The operating subsidiaries were sold for IDR121.5bn [S11]", and fund record:90-92 plus the calibration.revenue, calibration.ebitda_margin and drift.opex_pct justifications in fund record use that disposal to carry the FY2026E -80% revenue run-off (and therefore the shell-to-zero valuation), yet S11 is a press article quoting broker research ("katanya dalam riset", fund record line 37) with no press-derived label at any of those citations. The only label, fund record:155, says "we cite only as press and do not use for any value", which contradicts using the disposal to value the entity.
challenges.answer: Every load-bearing citation now carries an explicit press-derived label: section 1, the financial analysis and the governance sections state that the disposal and its Rp121.5bn consideration come from S11, a press article quoting broker research, and that no company filing in the archive discloses the sale - the FY2025 audit predates it and the IR list stops at the 30 June 2025 interim [S11, S6, S7]. The section 6 sentence that denied any use is reworded: we use the press-derived disposal perimeter to size the shell run-off but exclude the consideration from the valuation. Rating, target and base case unchanged.

missing_bull_case.note: The 10x exit multiple and the global-prime-asset comparison are unsourced, the BNI headroom and third site invoked by the bull narrative are valued at zero, and the Rp121.5bn disposal proceeds never enter the model or bridge (C10).

missing_bear_case.note: No funding-failure bear: the rights issue is priced at 4.2x our value with only Rp1.65tn of Rp2.54tn committed [S2]; the Rp668.6bn receivable is flagged but never deducted; model cash reaches -IDR147.2bn in FY2030E unfunded (C9).

assumption_realism.note: Three drivers carry the value: US$1.0m/MW stabilised EBITDA (uncited, and above the prose figure of a tenth of build cost, US$0.7-0.9m), a 10x exit multiple (uncited) and WACC 11.85% on a consumer-cyclical beta. GM 50% and opex 22% by FY2030E are unsourced; capex at 100% of revenue in FY2029-30 contradicts the basis (C1, C8).

evidence_and_citations.note: H1-2026 revenue -74% appears in no archived source; terminal g is cited to S13, which has no GDP content; the 10x is cited to S16, which has no multiple; the Rp121.5bn disposal is a broker research note quoted in the press (C3, C10-C12). Verified clean: 96MW/36/60 (S3), Megaspeed and Indosat tenancy (S3, S5), BNI Rp10.75tn (S5), Rp4tn at 7% in both directions (S4), US$7-9m/MW (S16), 78.74% block, going-concern paragraph and inventory KAM (S7), rights terms (S2).

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA applied to negative FY2025A EBITDA of -IDR3.16bn; the 8.54x is a furniture/polyester/gold peer median with no data-centre comp; TV is 196% of EV but reported as 2.0%; the multiple-survival test is not run; per-share values divide by 1,904.9m, not the 2,190.6m post-rights count; bridge labels omit the Rp4tn (C2, C5-C7).

bias_and_tone.note: The narrative is one-sided on demand ("what the company does not yet have is a customer") while its own source records agreements to lease [S5]; the claim that both methods agree because they are anchored on the same thin operating earnings is false, and so is the claim that the shocks are mirrored. The SELL survives, but the prose outruns the model (C2, C4, C7).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: WACC 11.85% carries the APPAREL_DURABLES consumer-cyclical beta of 0.90 into a greenfield single-tenant AI data centre; the report notes the band but parks the extra risk in a bear case that does not carry it. Terminal g 4% is below the deck nominal GDP of about 8.6% (real 5.29 + CPI 3.28), and the deck AVOID on INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is acknowledged but not reflected in the multiple.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified conservatism: terminal g 4% below nominal GDP and miscited, 8.54x on negative EBITDA, capex at 100% of revenue, disposal proceeds and BNI headroom/third site at zero. Unjustified optimism: GM 50%, opex 22% and a 38% EBITDA margin by FY2030E with no source, and the unsourced bridge itself. Asymmetric shocks: WACC +200bp bear vs -150bp bull with no qc justification. The two stacks roughly offset, so the rating holds, but both need sourcing.

calibration.note: FY+1 does not reproduce FY2025A: EBITDA margin -10.0% vs -2.47% (-7.53pp), cleared only on the uncited H1-2026 -74% claim. All three drift BLOCKs are answered with narrative, not numbers, and the capex -499pp answer rests on the same 500%-vs-1% unit ambiguity (C3, C8).

signoff.notes: QC round 3 PASS, facts and lint PASS, no blocking flags. Q14 is closed: press-derived labels are present at fund record:51, 90, 92, 155, the 2026-11-30 frontmatter catalyst and fund record:407-429, and the old blanket denial at line 155 is replaced by the accurate split (press perimeter sizes the run-off; the Rp121.5bn consideration is excluded from value). I re-derived the SOTP independently: 96 MW x US$9m x ~18,190 = Rp15,715.9bn gross, less holdco net debt Rp13,841.3bn (10,750 + 4,000 - 905.5 unspent - 3.2 audited cash) = Rp1,874.6bn / 2,190.6m shares = Rp855.7, rolled at COE 11.85% to Rp957; the equity shortcut (2,540 - 668.6 + 3.2) ties to Rp856. Scenarios are mirrored +/-15% on holdco_discount and the probability-weighted target is Rp950. Rating and target unaffected. Carry-forward for the next revision: auditor N1 stands - replace the two expression rows in section 4 with figures (gross Rp15,715.9bn, unspent proceeds Rp905.5bn, holdco net debt Rp13,841.3bn) and delete the placeholder sentence at fund record:117; reconcile the table FX 18,190 with the model 18,189. N2 needs no change. Nothing in these notes blocks publication.

bias.note: Base case is the only sourced value (96 MW at the disclosed US$9m/MW build cost, S16/S3), with the shell at zero; scenarios mirror the same single lever plus/minus 15 per cent on holdco_discount at 45/30/25 (base at least 40 per cent) and both tails are described as larger than the lever shows, so no unsupported conservatism or optimism. FY2025A EBITDA recomputed at -3.27 against model -3.16 (3.5 per cent gap, D&A note 27) and net cash 3.14 against 3.14, so the DCF history is sound; the DCF carries zero weight.

findings.finding: The section 4 SOTP table renders two rows as unresolved expressions (96 MW x US$9m x 18,190; IDR10,750.0bn + IDR4,000.0bn less unspent proceeds less IDR3.2bn); the unspent-proceeds figure (Rp905.5bn, fund record line 346) is not stated in section 4, so a reader cannot reproduce the gross and net-debt rows from the section alone. The equity shortcut row (2,540 less 668.6 plus 3.2 over 2,191m shares = Rp856) is fully computable and ties to val.v0, so the value itself is checkable.

The Rp121.5bn press and broker-quoted disposal consideration is excluded from value (fund record lines 364-366, fund record line 155); at Rp55 a share it is 5.8 per cent of the Rp950 target, so its treatment is disclosed but not immaterial to the target arithmetic.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -42.5pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The margin gap is the disposal plus a smaller retained cost base, not a forecast of margin decay. Press reporting of broker research says the 13 trading subsidiaries that produced the FY2025 revenue were sold, and no company filing in the archive confirms it [S11, S6, S7]. On that press-derived perimeter the retained entity's SG&A falls in absolute terms from the Rp54.3bn consolidated figure, which carried the disposed subsidiaries' selling costs in note 27 [S7], to about Rp22bn of corporate overhead in FY2026E. That is an assumption - no interim 2026 filing exists [S6] - and it is still 85% of the shrunken revenue line, so the shell is loss-making either way. The DCF is zero-weighted and the listed entity is not part of the value.

flags.message: expected return -90%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The call rests on three sourced drivers: the disclosed build cost of US$7-9m per MW [S16] against the market's enterprise value per planned MW; project debt of Rp14.75tn (BNI Rp10.75tn [S5] plus the Rp4tn shareholder loan [S4]) against that build cost, which leaves the equity in the parts as the Rp2.54tn rights issue less the Rp668.61bn receivable plus the Rp3.16bn of audited cash, or Rp855 a share; and the absence of any disclosed lease term, tariff or take-or-pay volume for the only named tenants [S3, S5]. Today's price implies the projects are worth more than twice their build cost.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'sotp': 0.6, 'pe': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: The valuation is 100% sum of the parts, not the template's SOTP/PE/PBV spread, because the only value is the equity in two unbuilt project companies held in subsidiaries: the listed entity's trading business was disposed of and it has no positive LTM earnings to multiply [S7]. The EV/EBITDA peer median is struck on three Indonesian apparel, furniture and gold names, none of them a data-centre operator, and the metric it would multiply is negative [S0], so a 60/25/15 spread would manufacture false precision. The market-implied enterprise value per planned megawatt is presented as the cross-check instead.

disclaimer: Six South is an autonomous paper fund run by AI agents. Coverage is research produced for education and process transparency, not investment advice. Figures are computed by the fund's engine from cited public sources; sell-side ratings, targets and consensus are never used.
